newsitem.title: UK: Suspected IRA bombs hit railway tracks, signals.
newsitem.headline: Suspected IRA bombs hit railway tracks, signals.

text.p: Two suspected IRA bombs damaged railway tracks and signalling equipment in the northwestern town of Wilmslow early on Wednesday in an apparent bid to cause disruption ahead of the May 1 British election.

Prime Minister John Major said the blasts looked very much like the work of the banned Irish Republican Army and called them a "two-fingered insult to democracy" in the run-up to the May 1 poll. There were no casualties.

"I hope very much that IRA/Sinn Fein are not going to conduct their campaigns at the ballot box in Northern Ireland and with bombs on the mainland of Britain," Major said before leaving London's Heathrow Airport for a campaign trip.

Sinn Fein is the political wing of the IRA, which is fighting to end British rule in Northern Ireland. The IRA has set off several bombs on the English mainland since ending a 17-month ceasefire in February 1996.

Wilmslow police said they had received coded warnings before the first blast hit a signalling box just outside the station at 6.30 a.m. (0630 GMT). The second blast damaged tracks at 7.05 a.m. (0705 GMT).

"These devices would appear to have been placed to cause disruption rather than physical injury," fire brigade spokesman Evan Morris told BBC radio. Police could not confirm the warnings had come from the IRA.
Wilmslow is a prosperous commuter town to the south of Manchester, where the IRA detonated a massive device in a city centre shopping precinct last June.
That blast, which injured 220 people, was the last known IRA attack on the mainland. The IRA have killed two soldiers in Northern Ireland since calling off their truce.
Eyewitnesses in Wilmslow spoke of two loud explosions early in the morning.

"We were woken up by an enormous bang at 6.30 a.m," Bridget Hunt told the BBC. "At 7 a.m. there was another even bigger explosion which rocked the ground...it was a terrific bang which shook the house," she said.
The blasts triggered speculation the IRA wanted to disrupt transport links, since Wilmslow is a major signalling point on the main railway line from London to northwest England.

The railway station at Doncaster was also shut down after coded warnings, but it was not immediately clear whether the two actions were linked. Doncaster is on the main railway line from London to the northeast of England.
"I think it's impossible to judge the minds of people who plant bombs indiscriminately and I find it very difficult to understand their mentality," Major said.

"Whether they're doing this because they think that in some warped perverted way that this will show their supporters that the IRA are still there as a real force -- I don't know," he added, calling on Sinn Fein to condemn the blasts.
"The (election) campaign certainly goes on. You can't extinguish democracy and the democratic process with bombs. You can't do it. It musn't be allowed to happen."
The bombs exploded ahead of the Easter weekend, which is one of the most sacred dates for the IRA, since it marks the anniversary of a major republican uprising in Dublin in 1916.
